claims.evidence: This is inferred from sequence analysis and comparison with other activating adaptors.

claims.claim: The Spindly motif in other activating adaptors binds to the pointed end of dynactin and facilitates dynein motility.
claims.source: Indeed, C-terminal to the CC in KASH5 is a putative Spindly motif, which in other activating adaptors binds to the pointed end of dynactin and facilitates dynein motility (Gama et al., 2017; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Processive dynein motility was observed in the presence of KASH5-ΔTM with purified components.
claims.source: Processive dynein motility was observed in the presence of KASH5-ΔTM (Figure 3E, G and H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F) but not in its absence (Figure 3G and H, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF experiments with purified proteins shown in Figure 3E, G, H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F.

claims.claim: Processive dynein motility was not observed in the absence of KASH5-ΔTM with purified components.
claims.source: Processive dynein motility was observed in the presence of KASH5-ΔTM (Figure 3E, G and H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F) but not in its absence (Figure 3G and H, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF experiments with purified proteins shown in Figure 3G, H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-G.

claims.claim: Moving Alexa-647 dynein was almost always colocalized with TMR-labeled KASH5-ΔTM.
claims.source: Moving Alexa-647 dynein was almost always colocalized with TMR-labeled KASH5-ΔTM (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF experiments with purified proteins shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: The velocity of processive events recorded with purified dynein, dynactin, and KASH5 was significantly slower than in the IP-TIRF motility experiments.
claims.source: The velocity of the processive events recorded with purified dynein, dynactin, and KASH5 was significantly slower than in the IP-TIRF motility experiments (median velocity of 0.320 µm/s with purified KASH5-ΔTM versus 0.538 µm/s with dynein immunoprecipitated by KASH5-ΔTM) (Figure 3C and G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of TIRF experiments with purified proteins versus IP-TIRF experiments shown in Figure 3C and G.

claims.claim: Lis1 increases the velocity of dynein-dynactin-activating adaptor motility.
claims.source: Lis1 increases the velocity of dynein-dynactin-activating adaptor motility by promoting dynein conformations that drive association with dynactin and an activating adaptor (Htet et al., 2020; Elshenawy et al., 2020; Gutierrez et al., 2017; Markus et al., 2020; Baumbach et al., 2017; Qiu et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Inclusion of purified Lis1 in the in vitro reconstituted TIRF experiments resulted in a significant increase in the velocity of motile events.
claims.source: Inclusion of purified Lis1 in the in vitro reconstituted TIRF experiments resulted in a significant increase in the velocity of motile events (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF experiments with purified proteins shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The velocity of dynein-dynactin-KASH5 processive events in the presence of Lis1 is comparable to that observed in the IP-TIRF motility experiments.
claims.source: In fact, the velocity of dynein-dynactin-KASH5 processive events in the presence of Lis1 is comparable to that observed in the IP-TIRF motility experiments (median velocity of 0.577 µm/s).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of TIRF experiments with purified proteins plus Lis1 versus IP-TIRF experiments.

claims.claim: Lis1 increases the landing rate, run length, and percent processivity of dynein-dynactin-KASH5 complexes.
claims.source: Consistent with observations made with other activating adaptors, Lis1 also increased the landing rate, run length, and percent processivity of dynein-dynactin-KASH5 complexes (Htet et al., 2020; Elshenawy et al., 2020; Gutierrez et al., 2017; Baumbach et al., 2017; Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF experiments with purified proteins shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, F.

claims.claim: Lis1 likely drives the association of dynein-dynactin-KASH5 complexes during meiosis.
claims.source: These data suggest that Lis1 likely drives the association of dynein-dynactin-KASH5 complexes during meiosis, as has been demonstrated for other activators in the cell (Htet et al., 2020; Qiu et al., 2019; Splinter et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Lis1 enhances KASH5-mediated dynein motility in vitro and from knowledge that Lis1 plays a similar role with other activating adaptors.

claims.claim: Nine conserved amino acids in the KASH5 EF-hand pair surround the hydrophobic surface of LIC harboring F447 and F448: I36, T40, Y60, V64, R73, L77, F97, L98, and M101.
claims.source: Based on this model, we identified nine conserved amino acids in the KASH5 EF-hand pair that surround the hydrophobic surface of LIC harboring F447 and F448 (Figure 4C): I36, T40, Y60, V64, R73, L77, F97, L98, and M101 (Figure 4A and C).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from a homology model based on the CRACR2a-LIC structure.

claims.claim: All the KASH5 EF-hand mutants tested showed impaired binding to dynein, albeit to varying extents.
claims.source: All the KASH5 EF-hand mutants tested showed impaired binding to dynein, albeit to varying extents (Figure 4D and E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 4D and E.

claims.claim: All the KASH5 EF-hand mutants co-precipitated at least some motile dynein.
claims.source: All the mutants co-precipitated at least some motile dynein, as visualized by GFP-KASH5-ΔTM-FLAG in TIRF (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by IP-TIRF experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Most of the KASH5 EF-hand mutants displayed motile events with comparable velocity, processivity, landing rate, and run length as WT KASH5-ΔTM.
claims.source: Most of the mutants displayed motile events with comparable velocity, processivity, landing rate, and run length as WT KASH5-ΔTM (Figure 4F–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by IP-TIRF experiments shown in Figure 4F–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B.

claims.claim: KASH5-ΔTML77D, KASH5-ΔTMF97D, and KASH5-ΔTMM101D displayed severely impaired dynein association and very little processive motility.
claims.source: However, three of the mutants, KASH5-ΔTML77D, KASH5-ΔTMF97D, and KASH5-ΔTMM101D displayed severely impaired dynein association and very little processive motility as visualized via TIRF (Figure 4D–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by co-IP and IP-TIRF experiments shown in Figure 4D–G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The velocity of the processive events observed for each KASH5 EF-hand mutant was not significantly different than KASH5-ΔTM.
claims.source: Though all KASH5 variants negatively affected binding to dynein, the velocity of the processive events that were observed for each mutant was not significantly different than KASH5-ΔTM (Figure 4F and H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by IP-TIRF experiments shown in Figure 4F and H.

claims.claim: The velocity of processive events for KASH5-ΔTML77D, KASH5-ΔTMF97D, and KASH5-ΔTMM101D was nearly identical to that induced by KASH5-ΔTM.
claims.source: Even for KASH5-ΔTML77D, KASH5-ΔTMF97D, and KASH5-ΔTMM101D, where we observed very few processive events, the velocity was nearly identical to that induced by KASH5-ΔTM (Figure 4G and H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by IP-TIRF experiments shown in Figure 4G, H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The binding between the EF-hand pair in dynein activating adaptors and the LIC promotes the formation of the activated dynein complex but is not required for fast, processive motility on microtubules.
claims.source: This result suggests that the binding between the EF-hand pair in dynein activating adaptors and the LIC promotes the formation of the activated dynein complex but that the activating adaptor-LIC interaction is not required for fast, processive motility on microtubules.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that mutants with impaired LIC binding still display normal velocity when processive events are observed.

claims.claim: SUN1-myc plus FLAG-KASH5-FL expression causes a significant increase in dynein enrichment at the NE relative to vehicle, SUN1-myc alone, or SUN1-myc plus Flag-KASH5-ΔTM controls.
claims.source: Indeed, SUN1-myc plus FLAG-KASH5-FL expression caused a significant increase in dynein enrichment at the NE relative to vehicle, SUN1-myc alone, or SUN1-myc plus Flag-KASH5-ΔTM controls (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in HeLa cells shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Expression of FLAG-tagged KASH5-FLL77D and KASH5-FLF97D significantly reduced the enrichment of GFP-dynein around the nuclear periphery.
claims.source: Quantitation of the data showed that expression of both FLAG-tagged KASH5-FLL77D and KASH5-FLF97D significantly reduced the enrichment of GFP-dynein around the nuclear periphery (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in HeLa cells shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: FLAG-KASH5-FLM101D reduced the ratio of GFP-dynein intensity at the NE versus cytoplasm compared to Flag-KASH5-FL, but the magnitude of the phenotype was not statistically significant.
claims.source: FLAG-KASH5-FLM101D also seemed to reduce the ratio of GFP-dynein intensity at the NE versus cytoplasm compared to Flag-KASH5-FL, but the magnitude of the phenotype was not statistically significant.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in HeLa cells shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: All three KASH5 mutant proteins (L77D, F97D, M101D) were more enriched at the NE than FLAG-KASH5-FL.
claims.source: We observed that all three KASH5 mutant proteins were more enriched at the NE than FLAG-KASH5-FL although the phenotype was not statistically significant for KASH5-FLF97D (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in HeLa cells shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Single mutations disrupting binding between KASH5's EF-hand pair and dynein's LIC are sufficient to disrupt dynein recruitment to the NE.
claims.source: Together, our intracellular localization experiments in HeLa cells show that single mutations disrupting binding between KASH5's EF-hand pair and dynein's LIC are sufficient to disrupt dynein recruitment to the NE.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the immunofluorescence experiments in HeLa cells showing reduced dynein localization at the NE with KASH5 mutants.

claims.claim: KASH5 acts specifically in meiotic prophase I to facilitate telomere motility along the NE.
claims.source: KASH5 acts specifically in meiotic prophase I to facilitate telomere motility along the NE (Morimoto et al., 2012; Horn et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Full-length KASH5 and all three mutants (L147D, F167D, M171D) localize to meiotic telomeres.
claims.source: Full-length KASH5 and all three mutants localize to meiotic telomeres, confirming that the mutations do not perturb binding of KASH5 to SUN1 or SUN1 to the telomeres (Morimoto et al., 2012; Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in mouse spermatocytes shown in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: The mutations in KASH5 do not perturb binding of KASH5 to SUN1 or SUN1 to the telomeres.
claims.source: Full-length KASH5 and all three mutants localize to meiotic telomeres, confirming that the mutations do not perturb binding of KASH5 to SUN1 or SUN1 to the telomeres (Morimoto et al., 2012; Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that all KASH5 mutants localize to telomeres.

claims.claim: The staining of endogenous dynactin subunit p150 at telomeres was significantly decreased in spermatocytes expressing GFP-KASH5L147D.
claims.source: However, the staining of endogenous dynactin subunit p150 at telomeres was significantly decreased in spermatocytes expressing GFP-KASH5L147D (the telomere-localized p150 signal intensity in the mutant-expressing cells was 73% that of cells not expressing any GFP-tagged protein), suggesting that a single mutation in the KASH5-dynein interface is sufficient to disrupt the localization of the dynein transport machinery in a dominant fashion in WT spermatocytes (Figure 6A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in mouse spermatocytes shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: A single mutation in the KASH5-dynein interface is sufficient to disrupt the localization of the dynein transport machinery in a dominant fashion in WT spermatocytes.
claims.source: However, the staining of endogenous dynactin subunit p150 at telomeres was significantly decreased in spermatocytes expressing GFP-KASH5L147D (the telomere-localized p150 signal intensity in the mutant-expressing cells was 73% that of cells not expressing any GFP-tagged protein), suggesting that a single mutation in the KASH5-dynein interface is sufficient to disrupt the localization of the dynein transport machinery in a dominant fashion in WT spermatocytes (Figure 6A and B).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GFP-KASH5L147D expression reduces p150 localization at telomeres in the presence of endogenous KASH5.

claims.claim: GFP-KASH5F167D and GFP-KASH5M171D mutants did not cause dominant phenotypes in mouse spermatocytes.
claims.source: The GFP-KASH5F167D and GFP-KASH5M171D mutants did not cause dominant phenotypes, although they are expressed (as assessed by western blot; Figure 6C) and enriched at telomeres (as assessed by GFP foci intensity at telomeres; Figure 6D) to the same extent at GFP-tagged KASH5 WT and L147D proteins.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in mouse spermatocytes shown in Figure 6A, B, C, and D.

claims.claim: The triple mutant L147D-F167D-M171D decreased p150 accumulation at telomeres in mouse spermatocytes.
claims.source: The triple mutant, but not the double mutant, decreased p150 accumulation at telomeres, suggesting that the F167D and M171D mutations do not substantially alter dynein-dynactin localization to telomeres in mouse spermatocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in mouse spermatocytes shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C.

claims.claim: The F167D and M171D mutations do not substantially alter dynein-dynactin localization to telomeres in mouse spermatocytes.
claims.source: The triple mutant, but not the double mutant, decreased p150 accumulation at telomeres, suggesting that the F167D and M171D mutations do not substantially alter dynein-dynactin localization to telomeres in mouse spermatocytes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the double mutant F167D-M171D does not reduce p150 localization at telomeres.

claims.claim: Human KASH5 L77 (mouse KASH5 L147) is central to KASH5-dynein binding and KASH5 recruitment to the NE.
claims.source: Together, our results suggest that human KASH5 L77 (mouse KASH5 L147) is central to KASH5-dynein binding and KASH5 recruitment to the NE.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the L77D (L147D in mouse) mutation has the most consistent and significant effect on dynein binding and localization across all experimental systems.

claims.claim: KASH5 is unique among known activating adaptors because it is the first known TM domain-containing activating adaptor.
claims.source: KASH5 is unique among known activating adaptors for several reasons. First, it is the first known TM domain-containing activating adaptor.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the domain structure of KASH5 and knowledge of other activating adaptors.

claims.claim: Other activating adaptors that link dynein to membranous cargos do so via a receptor protein associated with the cargo lipids.
claims.source: Other activating adaptors that link dynein to membranous cargos do so via a receptor protein (e.g. Rabs) associated with the cargo lipids (Huynh and Vale, 2017; Horgan and McCaffrey, 2011; Jordens et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: KASH5 is the first known activating adaptor in the KASH (or Nesprin) family of SUN-binding proteins.
claims.source: Second, KASH5 is the first known activating adaptor in the KASH (or Nesprin) family of SUN-binding proteins.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of the KASH protein family and the finding that KASH5 is an activating adaptor.

claims.claim: Other KASH proteins, like KASH2 (also called Nesprin-2), promote dynein localization to the nucleus during nuclear migration by engaging activating adaptors like BicD2.
claims.source: Other KASH proteins, like KASH2 (also called Nesprin-2), promote dynein localization to the nucleus during nuclear migration by engaging activating adaptors like BicD2 (Gonçalves et al., 2020; Tsai et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: KASH5 directly binds dynein to form an activated dynein complex at the NE.
claims.source: KASH5 directly binds dynein to form an activated dynein complex at the NE.
claims.evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental approaches.

claims.claim: KASH5 is the only known meiosis-specific activating adaptor.
claims.source: Third, KASH5 is the only known meiosis-specific activating adaptor, consistent with the unique cargo it moves.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the meiosis-specific expression of KASH5 and knowledge of other activating adaptors.

claims.claim: Mammalian telomeres are generally dispersed in the nucleoplasm at steady-state in all somatic and germ cells, except in spermatocytes (or oocytes) undergoing meiosis.
claims.source: Mammalian telomeres are generally dispersed in the nucleoplasm at steady-state in all somatic and germ cells, except in spermatocytes (or oocytes) undergoing meiosis (Shibuya and Watanabe, 2014c; Palm and de Lange, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: Homologous chromosome pairing in prophase I of meiosis requires the relocalization of all telomeres to the NE of spermatocytes to connect chromosomes to cytosolic dynein.
claims.source: Homologous chromosome pairing in prophase I of meiosis requires the relocalization of all telomeres to the NE of spermatocytes to connect chromosomes to cytosolic dynein.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: The two copies of KASH5 EF-hand pairs from one KASH5 homodimer interact with one LIC polypeptide.
claims.source: Interestingly, our SEC-MALS data support a model where the two copies of KASH5 EF-hand pairs from one KASH5 homodimer interact with one LIC polypeptide.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the 2:1 stoichiometry observed in SEC-MALS experiments.

claims.claim: The 2:1 stoichiometry of KASH5 to LIC is different than what has been captured in LIC helix 1 peptide-bound crystal structures of LIC-binding domains of HOOK3 and CRACR2A, which reveal a 1:1 stoichiometry.
claims.source: This stoichiometry is different than what has been captured in LIC helix 1 peptide-bound crystal structures of LIC-binding domains of HOOK3 and CRACR2A, which reveal a 1:1 stoichiometry (Lee et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparison of the SEC-MALS data with published crystal structures.

claims.claim: The HOOK3 HOOK-LIC helix 1 and the CRACR2A EF-hand pair-LIC helix 1 structures were solved in the context of the N-terminal activating adaptor domains that lack the downstream CC responsible for homodimerization.
claims.source: However, the HOOK3 HOOK-LIC helix 1 (PDB: 6BPH) (Lee et al., 2018) and the CRACR2A EF-hand pair-LIC helix 1(PDB: 6PSD) (Lee et al., 2020) structures were solved in the context of the N-terminal activating adaptor domains that lack the downstream CC responsible for homodimerization.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from published crystal structures.

claims.claim: The absence of dimerization may have prevented the capture of the 2:1 stoichiometry of the activator-LIC helix complex in the HOOK3 and CRACR2A crystal structures.
claims.source: It is possible that the absence of dimerization may have prevented the capture of the 2:1 stoichiometry of the activator-LIC helix complex in these structures.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the difference between the crystal structures and the SEC-MALS data.

claims.claim: BicD2 uses a dimeric N-terminal CC-box to bind LIC.
claims.source: Interestingly, BicD2 uses a dimeric N-terminal CC-box to bind LIC.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The structure of the BicD2 N-terminal CC with the LIC helix 1 shows binding of two BicD2 CC helices to a single LIC helix.
claims.source: The structure of the BicD2 N-terminal CC with the LIC helix 1 (PDB: 6PSE) shows binding of two BicD2 CC helices to a single LIC helix (Lee et al., 2020); however, it was suggested that crystal packing may have prevented the binding of the second LIC helix to the BicD2 dimer.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from a published crystal structure.

claims.claim: A 2:2 BicD2-LIC helix interaction was inferred from ITC experiments.
claims.source: Indeed, a 2:2 BicD2-LIC helix interaction was inferred from ITC experiments in the same study (Lee et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from a published study.

claims.claim: A cryo-EM reconstitution of the dynein-dynactin complex including full-length LIC with BICDR1 captured two BICDR1 homodimers bound to the dimeric dynein complex.
claims.source: In this regard, a recent preprint describes a cryo-EM reconstitution of the dynein-dynactin complex including full-length LIC with another BicD family activator, BICDR1 (Chaaban and Carter, 2022). This study captured two BICDR1 homodimers bound to the dimeric dynein complex.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from a recent preprint.

claims.claim: In the cryo-EM structure of dynein-dynactin-BICDR1, evidence from the EM maps for binding of the first LIC molecule was clear, but density for the second LIC was either less resolved or absent.
claims.source: While evidence from the EM maps for binding of the first LIC molecule was clear, density for the second LIC was either less resolved (for BICDR-A homodimer) or absent (for BICDR-B homodimer).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from a recent preprint.

claims.claim: Although there are two binding sites for a standalone LIC helix on dimeric activating adaptors, binding of the first full-length LIC could affect the affinity/accessibility of the second LIC polypeptide for its binding site on an activating adaptor.
claims.source: Together, these results suggest that although there are two binding sites for a standalone LIC helix on dimeric activating adaptors, binding of the first full-length LIC could affect the affinity/accessibility of the second LIC polypeptide for its binding site on an activating adaptor.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combination of structural and biochemical data from multiple studies.

claims.claim: The dimeric structure of KASH5 is consistent with its role as a dynein activating adaptor.
claims.source: While the dimeric structure of KASH5 is consistent with its role as a dynein activating adaptor, it raises interesting questions about SUN1-KASH5 quaternary structure and its implications for chromosome motility.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that KASH5 is dimeric and knowledge that other activating adaptors are also dimeric.

claims.claim: SUN proteins are known to trimerize.
claims.source: SUN proteins are known to trimerize (Sosa et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The trimerization of SUN proteins creates a potential stoichiometry mismatch between SUN1 and KASH5 that can promote higher-order quaternary structures.
claims.source: This creates a potential stoichiometry mismatch between SUN1 and KASH5 that can promote higher-order quaternary structures.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the knowledge that SUN1 trimerizes and KASH5 dimerizes.

claims.claim: Binding to KASH peptides (from KASH1, KASH4, and KASH5) induces two SUN1 trimers to bind head-to-head to form a 6:6 SUN-KASH complex.
claims.source: A recent study demonstrated that binding to KASH peptides (from KASH1, KASH4, and KASH5) induces two SUN1 trimers to bind head-to-head to form a 6:6 SUN-KASH complex (Gurusaran and Davies, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Higher-order SUN1-KASH5 structures might facilitate the recruitment of multiple dynein motors and the generation of large forces needed to move chromosomes across the NE.
claims.source: These higher-order structures might facilitate the recruitment of multiple dynein motors and the generation of large forces needed to move chromosomes across the NE.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the potential for higher-order structures.

claims.claim: When dynein-dynactin-KASH5 motility was reconstituted in vitro, the activated dynein complex formed less robustly and generated complexes that moved with a significantly slower velocity unless Lis1 was present.
claims.source: However, when we reconstituted dynein-dynactin-KASH5 motility in vitro, the activated dynein complex formed less robustly and generated complexes that moved with a significantly slower velocity unless Lis1 was present.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by TIRF experiments with purified proteins.

claims.claim: Lis1 is key to forming the activated dynein-dynactin-KASH5 complexes.
claims.source: This result suggests that Lis1 is key to forming the activated dynein-dynactin-KASH5 complexes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Lis1 enhances the formation and velocity of dynein-dynactin-KASH5 complexes.

claims.claim: Lis1 is involved in dynein's meiosis-specific function.
claims.source: Furthermore, our studies suggest that Lis1 is involved in dynein's meiosis-specific function, providing new insights into an understudied area of dynein research.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Lis1 enhances KASH5-mediated dynein motility.

claims.claim: The velocity of the immunoprecipitated dynein-dynactin-KASH5 complexes was comparable for all the KASH5 EF-hand mutants tested, regardless of their ability to bind KASH5.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found that the velocity of the immunoprecipitated dynein-dynactin-KASH5 complexes was comparable for all the mutants tested, regardless of their ability to bind KASH5.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by IP-TIRF experiments.

claims.claim: Binding between activating adaptors and dynein LIC promotes the formation of the dynein-dynactin-activator complex but does not affect the velocity of the activated complex.
claims.source: This result suggests that binding between activating adaptors and dynein LIC promotes the formation of the dynein-dynactin-activator complex but does not affect the velocity of the activated complex.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that KASH5 mutants with impaired LIC binding still display normal velocity when processive events are observed.

claims.claim: KASH5's TM domain is required for robust nuclear localization of KASH5 and recruitment of dynein to the NE.
claims.source: Our results confirm that KASH5's TM domain is required for robust nuclear localization of KASH5 and recruitment of dynein there, consistent with previous studies (Horn et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in HeLa cells and supported by previous studies.

claims.claim: KASH5 localization at the NE is dependent on SUN1 but independent of dynein binding.
claims.source: Interestingly, KASH5 localization at the NE is dependent on SUN1 but independent of dynein binding, suggesting that it could occur before, or concomitant with, dynein recruitment to the NE in meiotic prophase I.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in HeLa cells.

claims.claim: KASH5 localization at the NE could occur before, or concomitant with, dynein recruitment to the NE in meiotic prophase I.
claims.source: Interestingly, KASH5 localization at the NE is dependent on SUN1 but independent of dynein binding, suggesting that it could occur before, or concomitant with, dynein recruitment to the NE in meiotic prophase I.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that KASH5 localization at the NE is independent of dynein binding.

claims.claim: A single mutation at the interface between KASH5's EF-hand domain and dynein's LIC is sufficient to prevent dynein localization to the outer nuclear membrane both in HeLa cells and mouse spermatocytes transiently expressing KASH5 protein.
claims.source: Finally, it is impressive that a single mutation at the interface between KASH5's EF-hand domain and dynein's LIC is sufficient to prevent dynein localization to the outer nuclear membrane both in HeLa cells and mouse spermatocytes transiently expressing KASH5 protein.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence experiments in HeLa cells and mouse spermatocytes.

claims.claim: Meiosis-specific proteins, protein isoforms, and post-translational modifications in dynein may partly compensate for the weakened NCC-LIC interaction in vivo.
claims.source: Alternatively, or in addition, meiosis-specific proteins, protein isoforms, and post-translational modifications in dynein may partly compensate for the weakened NCC-LIC interaction.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the reason for the milder phenotype in vivo.

claims.claim: Contributions of the EF-hand residues may be different in human versus mouse cells, potentially underlying a previously uncharacterized species-specificity for dynein activation in meiosis.
claims.source: Finally, we cannot rule out the possibility that contributions of the EF-hand residues may be different in human versus mouse cells, potentially underlying a previously uncharacterized species-specificity for dynein activation in meiosis.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential species-specific differences.

claims.claim: Mouse KASH5 harbors a 70 amino acid N-terminal extension absent in other mammalian homologs, including human KASH5.
claims.source: In this regard, mouse KASH5 harbors a 70 amino acid N-terminal extension absent in other mammalian homologs, including human KASH5, and whose significance remains unknown (Morimoto et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: The KASH5-dynein interaction is important for coupling telomeres to the cytoskeletal machinery in prophase I of meiosis.

results.result: KASH5 directly binds dynein's light-intermediate chain (LIC) using a conserved mechanism. The KASH5 N-terminal domain and NCC construct bind LIC directly, while the CC domain alone does not. KASH5-NCC co-elutes with LIC in size exclusion chromatography, and this interaction is disrupted by the LIC F447A/F448A mutation, indicating KASH5 uses a structural mechanism shared with other dynein activating adaptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C41 are well-supported by multiple complementary biochemical approaches including co-immunoprecipitation (C30-C32), direct binding assays (C34-C35), size exclusion chromatography (C37, C40), and mutational analysis (C40-C41). The data consistently demonstrate that KASH5 binds dynein LIC through its N-terminal domain using a conserved mechanism involving the LIC F447/F448 residues.

results.result: KASH5 forms a homodimer and binds LIC with a 2:1 stoichiometry. SEC-MALS analysis shows that KASH5-NCC is a homodimer with an experimentally determined molecular weight of 139 kDa, consistent with a 2:1 NCC:LIC stoichiometry. This stoichiometry persists at high protein concentrations and with excess LIC. Dimeric KASH5 EF-hands bind a single copy of LIC.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C54 are strongly supported by SEC-MALS data (C42-C45, C48-C52) showing consistent 2:1 stoichiometry under multiple conditions. The use of both dimeric (GST-tagged) and monomeric (untagged) KASH5-N constructs provides compelling evidence that dimeric KASH5 binds a single LIC molecule (C52-C54). The experimental molecular weights closely match theoretical predictions.

results.result: KASH5-NCC binds the LIC peptide with a dissociation constant Kd = 4.3 μM, comparable to other activating adaptors. The KASH5 EF-hand pair does not bind Ca2+, and Ca2+ does not regulate the NCC-LIC interaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C58 are well-supported by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) experiments. The measured Kd of 4.3 μM is within the range reported for other activating adaptors (C55-C56). ITC experiments in the presence of CaCl2 or EGTA show similar dissociation constants (C57), and titration of Ca2+ into KASH5-NCC shows no enthalpy change (C58), providing strong evidence that Ca2+ does not regulate this interaction.

results.result: KASH5 converts dynein into a processive motor. IP-TIRF experiments show that GFP-KASH5-ΔTM-FLAG and GFP-KASH5-NCC-FLAG display processive movements on microtubules at velocities ~0.5 μm/s. Reconstitution with purified components confirms that processive dynein motility requires KASH5-ΔTM, with moving dynein colocalized with labeled KASH5.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C68 are strongly supported by both IP-TIRF experiments with cell lysates (C59-C62) and reconstitution experiments with purified proteins (C66-C68). The observation of processive movement at physiologically relevant velocities, the requirement for KASH5 in purified systems, and the colocalization of dynein and KASH5 provide compelling evidence that KASH5 activates dynein motility. The slight differences between KASH5 constructs (C61-C63) are appropriately noted.

results.result: Lis1 enhances dynein-dynactin-KASH5 complex formation and motility. Purified dynein-dynactin-KASH5 complexes move slower than IP-TIRF complexes unless Lis1 is present. Addition of Lis1 significantly increases velocity, landing rate, run length, and processivity of dynein-dynactin-KASH5 complexes to levels comparable to IP-TIRF experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C74 and C120-C122 are well-supported by TIRF experiments comparing purified proteins with and without Lis1. The significant increase in velocity (from 0.320 to 0.577 μm/s) and other motility parameters upon Lis1 addition (C71-C73) provides strong evidence for Lis1's role. The inference that Lis1 is involved in dynein's meiosis-specific function (C74, C122) is reasonable but represents an extrapolation from in vitro data.

results.result: Specific residues in the KASH5 EF-hand pair mediate dynein binding but not motor velocity. Nine conserved amino acids were identified through homology modeling. All mutants showed impaired dynein binding to varying extents, with L77D, F97D, and M101D showing the most severe defects. However, the velocity of processive events was not significantly different from wild-type for any mutant, suggesting that the EF-hand-LIC interaction promotes complex formation but is not required for processive motility.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C82 and C123-C124 are supported by co-IP experiments (C76), IP-TIRF motility assays (C77-C81), and velocity measurements (C80-C81). The identification of critical residues through homology modeling (C75) is reasonable given the conservation with CRACR2a. The key finding that mutants with impaired binding still display normal velocity when processive events occur (C80-C82, C123-C124) is well-documented, though the mechanistic interpretation requires further investigation.

results.result: Disrupting the KASH5-LIC interaction impairs dynein recruitment to the nuclear envelope in HeLa cells. Expression of SUN1-myc plus FLAG-KASH5-FL significantly increases dynein enrichment at the NE. KASH5 mutants L77D and F97D significantly reduce dynein enrichment at the NE, while increasing KASH5 enrichment at the NE. KASH5 localization at the NE is dependent on SUN1 but independent of dynein binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 and C125-C128 are well-supported by immunofluorescence experiments in HeLa cells. The quantification of NE:cytoplasm ratios for both dynein and KASH5 provides robust evidence (C83-C86). The observation that KASH5 mutants localize to the NE despite impaired dynein binding (C86, C126) is particularly informative. However, the statistical significance for M101D is marginal (C85), which is appropriately noted.

results.result: Disrupting the KASH5-LIC interaction reduces dynein-dynactin localization to telomeres in mouse spermatocytes. All KASH5 mutants (L147D, F167D, M171D) localize to meiotic telomeres, confirming that mutations do not affect KASH5-SUN1 or SUN1-telomere binding. GFP-KASH5L147D significantly decreases p150 staining at telomeres (73% of control), while F167D and M171D do not show dominant phenotypes. The triple mutant, but not the double mutant, decreases p150 accumulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C96 are supported by immunofluorescence experiments in mouse spermatocytes. The localization of all mutants to telomeres (C89-C90) validates the experimental approach. The dominant-negative effect of L147D (C91-C92) is statistically significant and biologically meaningful. The lack of phenotype for F167D and M171D individually (C93, C95) but presence in the triple mutant (C94) suggests these residues have weaker contributions, which is consistent with the in vitro data.

results.result: KASH5 is a unique dynein activating adaptor with several distinctive features. It is the first known transmembrane domain-containing activating adaptor, the first activating adaptor in the KASH/Nesprin family, and the only known meiosis-specific activating adaptor. Unlike other KASH proteins that engage activating adaptors like BicD2, KASH5 directly binds dynein to form an activated complex at the nuclear envelope.
results.evaluation: Claims C11 and C97-C102 are supported by the combined experimental evidence demonstrating KASH5's activating adaptor function and knowledge of other activating adaptors and KASH proteins. The uniqueness claims (C11, C97, C99, C102) are appropriately qualified by 'first known' or 'only known,' acknowledging the possibility of future discoveries. The comparison with other KASH proteins (C98, C100) is supported by citations.

results.result: The 2:1 KASH5:LIC stoichiometry differs from crystal structures of other activating adaptors but may reflect the use of full-length LIC versus peptides. Crystal structures of HOOK3 and CRACR2A with LIC peptides show 1:1 stoichiometry, while BicD2 shows 2:1 binding to a single LIC helix. Recent cryo-EM data with full-length LIC and BICDR1 shows variable LIC density, suggesting that binding of the first full-length LIC may affect accessibility of the second binding site.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C114 provide a thoughtful discussion of the stoichiometry findings in the context of published structures. The comparison with crystal structures (C106-C111) is accurate based on the cited literature. The speculation about the role of full-length LIC versus peptides (C108, C114) is reasonable and supported by the recent cryo-EM data (C112-C113). However, C108 is explicitly labeled as speculation, which is appropriate.

results.result: The dimeric structure of KASH5 and trimeric structure of SUN1 create a potential stoichiometry mismatch that may promote higher-order quaternary structures. A recent study showed that KASH peptides induce two SUN1 trimers to form a 6:6 SUN-KASH complex. These higher-order structures might facilitate recruitment of multiple dynein motors and generation of large forces needed to move chromosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C119 present an interesting hypothesis about higher-order structures, but the evidence is limited. While the dimeric nature of KASH5 is established (C115) and SUN1 trimerization is known (C116), the formation of 6:6 complexes was demonstrated with KASH peptides (C118), not full-length KASH5. The speculation about force generation (C119) is reasonable but lacks direct experimental support. This represents an interesting area for future investigation but is not directly demonstrated in this study.

results.result: The KASH5-dynein interaction is important for coupling telomeres to the cytoskeletal machinery in prophase I of meiosis, which is a prerequisite for meiotic progression and mammalian fertility.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C134 are supported by the combined results showing that disrupting the KASH5-dynein interaction impairs dynein localization to telomeres in mouse spermatocytes. While the study does not directly test fertility outcomes, the importance of telomere-cytoskeleton coupling for meiosis is well-established in the field (C134), and the data clearly demonstrate that KASH5-dynein binding is critical for this process (C133).
